title: PRP Versus NP Injections for Chronic Discogenic Low Back Pain
official: Randomized, Comparative-Effectiveness Study of Intradiscal Injections for Chronic Discogenic Low Back Pain (LBP)
summary:
The purpose of this randomized, single-blind comparative-effectiveness pilot study is to compare the effectiveness of two types of injections on pain and function over 6 months in patients with chronic discogenic (originating from the intervertebral discs) low back pain (LBP). Eligible participants will have failed an adequate trial of previous conservative treatments, had no prior surgery, and had no prior injections within the preceding 12 months of study participation.

One of the treatments in this study is called platelet-rich plasma (PRP). It uses a sample of a participant's own blood, which is spun in a machine to concentrate the platelets. These platelets are then injected into the participant's back to help healing and reduce pain and swelling. The other treatment available in this study uses donor tissue from the center of a spinal disc, called the nucleus pulposus (NP). This gel-like material normally helps absorb shock in the spine. In this therapy, NP tissue from a donor is injected into the damaged disc to help restore its cushioning function and replace lost tissue. In this study, participants will be randomly assigned to receive one of the two injections (either PRP or NP) to treat chronic discogenic LBP. In order to limit bias in outcome data, participants will not know what injection they received until 6 months post-procedure.

Participants will be asked to complete between 5-6 in-person visits with the study team. Beyond procedure-related activities including a blood draw and injection, participants will also complete questionnaires and physical examinations at the respective study visits.
criteria:
Inclusion Criteria:

* Can read and understand English
* DEERS eligible
* Ages 18-100
* Low back pain duration \> 3 months
* Failed an adequate trial of previous conservative treatments for \> 3 months including PT, and oral analgesics, anti-inflammatory medications, or injection therapy within the past 12 months
* Average pain score ≥ 4/10 over the past week
* Presumed clinical diagnosis of discogenic LBP (such as central, midline back pain exacerbated with flexion and loading; non-radiating; normal sensorimotor exam)
* Lumbar MRI within the last 12 months showing disc degeneration in ≤ 2 lumbar discs; Modified Pfirrmann scoring III-VII
* Agrees to have disc injection(s) and no other low back interventional (e.g., lumbar epidural steroid injections) or new pharmacological treatments (other than permitted supplemental medications which must be stopped 2 weeks prior to each follow-up) outside of the study for at least 6 months \[Physical therapy (PT), exercise, or psychotherapy are allowed prior to 6 months\]
* Agrees to be off all NSAIDs (e.g., aspirin, ibuprofen, Aleve, naproxen, Advil, Motrin, Celebrex) from 2 weeks prior to and 3 months after the injection
* Agrees to be off all corticosteroids (e.g., systemic, other injections) for at least 6 weeks after the injection
* Stable dose of analgesic medications (excluding NSAIDs) for at least 2 weeks (off schedule 2 opioids for 1 month)

Exclusion Criteria:

* Pregnancy (Women of childbearing capacity will have pregnancy test to confirm status)
* Actively breastfeeding
* Low back pain \> 15 years in duration
* Previous disc directed therapy involving heat (e.g., Intradiscal electrothermal therapy (IDET), biacuplasty)
* Previous disc injection therapy in the last 12 months (e.g., corticosteroid, PRP)
* Corticosteroid injections of the low back in the 3 months prior to injection and other corticosteroid therapy (e.g., systemic, other injections) in the 6 weeks prior to injection
* Previous lumbar spine surgery (e.g., discectomy, fusion) at the affected levels (i.e., those with relief after surgery in whom adjacent segment discogenic pain is suspected can be considered on a case-by-case basis)
* Focal neurological deficit attributed to disc pathology (i.e., abnormal sensorimotor exam consistent with disc pathology)
* Individuals deemed at risk to require systemic steroid over the 6-month study course (e.g., individuals with poorly controlled asthma or COPD, individuals with a poorly controlled autoimmune disease)
* Individuals with poorly controlled medical or psychiatric co-morbidities, as determined by their specialist or primary care provider (in those not receiving specialty care)
* Poorly controlled medical (e.g., unstable angina, congestive heart failure, poorly controlled diabetes) or psychiatric condition that has required medication adjustments within the past 2 weeks (severe depression or schizophrenia)
* Untreated coagulopathy or inability to safely stop anticoagulants
* Allergy to contrast dye or local anesthetics
* Inability to stop Schedule 2 opioid use within 1 month of enrollment due to chronic pain
* Diffuse pain phenotype (e.g., diagnosis of fibromyalgia)
* Secondary gain (e.g., ongoing medical board or litigation related to injury)
* Anticipated PCS or deployment within 12 months of enrollment
